title: What is Kafka? Topics, partitions, offsets? Consumer groups? Producer acks/idempotence? At-least-once/at-most-once/exactly-once? Dead Letter Topic? Kafka Streams? Schema Registry? Kafka Connect? Spring Kafka (@KafkaListener, KafkaTemplate)?
shortTitle: Kafka — producer/consumer, partitions, consumer groups, exactly-once, DLT, Spring Kafka

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Topics categorize events. Partitions provide parallelism (one partition = one consumer per group). Offsets track position. Producer `acks=all` + `enable.idempotence=true` ensures no data loss and no duplicates. Consumer groups enable parallel consumption: each partition read by exactly one consumer in the group. At-least-once: process then commit offset (most common — consumer must be idempotent). Dead Letter Topic (DLT): failed messages after max retries go to a separate topic for inspection. `@RetryableTopic` automates retry + DLT in Spring Kafka. Schema Registry (Avro/Protobuf) ensures producer-consumer schema compatibility.
s1_definition.analogy: Kafka is the bank's internal mail system. Topics = mailboxes ("payment-events", "trade-events"). Partitions = slots in each mailbox (parallel processing). Consumer groups = teams reading mail — each letter read by exactly one team member. DLT = the "undeliverable" drawer for letters that nobody can process after 3 attempts.
s1_definition.oneliner: Topics for categories. Partitions for parallelism. Consumer groups for parallel consumption. acks=all for durability. Idempotent consumer for at-least-once. DLT for poison pills. Schema Registry for compatibility.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Topics categorize events. Partitions provide parallelism (one partition = one consumer per group). Offsets track position. Producer `acks=all` + `enable.idempotence=true` ensures no data loss and no duplicates. Consumer groups enable parallel consumption: each partition read by exactly one consumer in the group. At-least-once: process then commit offset (most common — consumer must be idempotent). Dead Letter Topic (DLT): failed messages after max retries go to a separate topic for inspection. `@RetryableTopic` automates retry + DLT in Spring Kafka. Schema Registry (Avro/Protobuf) ensures producer-consumer schema compatibility.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Kafka is the bank's internal mail system. Topics = mailboxes ("payment-events", "trade-events"). Partitions = slots in each mailbox (parallel processing). Consumer groups = teams reading mail — each letter read by exactly one team member. DLT = the "undeliverable" drawer for letters that nobody can process after 3 attempts.

**One line to remember:** Topics for categories. Partitions for parallelism. Consumer groups for parallel consumption. acks=all for durability. Idempotent consumer for at-least-once. DLT for poison pills. Schema Registry for compatibility.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me explain Kafka calmly, the way I would to a junior developer sitting next to me, starting from the very basics and building up to the senior-level nuances.

A Kafka topic is a named stream of events, like a category of mail. In our banking platform we have a topic called trade-events. Every trade that happens in the bank becomes an event written to this topic. A topic is split into partitions, and partitions are the real secret to Kafka's scale. A partition is an append-only, ordered log — messages are added at the end and each gets a sequential number called an offset. Ordering is guaranteed only within a single partition, never across partitions. When you create a topic you choose how many partitions it has. We chose six, which means up to six consumers can read in parallel.

The producer decides which partition a message goes to using the message key. When the producer calls `kafkaTemplate.send("trade-events", accountId, event)`, the account id is the key. Kafka hashes the key and always maps the same key to the same partition. This is why we key by account id — all of Rajesh's trades stay on one partition and therefore stay in order. For example, `kafkaTemplate.send("trade-events", "SAV2001", tradeEvent)` guarantees that two trades from SAV2001 are never reordered, because they live on the same partition.

Producer durability is controlled by the `acks` setting. With `acks=all`, the producer waits until the partition leader and all in-sync replicas have written the message before it considers the send successful; this is how you avoid losing data if a broker dies. For example, in application.yml we set `acks: all` together with `retries: 3`. Retries alone can cause duplicates, so we also set `enable.idempotence=true`, which makes the broker recognise and discard a retried message that it has already stored. In code this is just configuration: `props.put("enable.idempotence", true)`.

Consumer groups are how Kafka shares work. A consumer group is a team identified by a group id, such as settlement-group. Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within the group, so a message is processed once per group. If you have six partitions and three consumers, each consumer handles two partitions. If a consumer dies, Kafka rebalances and gives its partitions to the survivors. For example, `@KafkaListener(topics = "trade-events", groupId = "settlement-group", concurrency = "3")` starts three consumer threads in one group. A key rule: you can never have more active consumers than partitions — extra consumers just sit idle.

Delivery semantics come down to when you commit the offset. At-most-once commits the offset before processing, so a crash loses the message — dangerous for money. At-least-once processes first and commits afterwards, so a crash replays the message, which is safe only if the consumer is idempotent. Exactly-once is achievable with Kafka transactions and the `read_process_write` pattern, but in practice most banking consumers use at-least-once plus an idempotency check. We disable auto commit with `enable-auto-commit: false` and commit manually with `ack.acknowledge()` only after the settlement is saved.

Idempotency on the consumer side is non-negotiable when you use at-least-once. We enforce it two ways: a cheap application check `settlementRepo.existsByTradeId(tradeId)` before processing, and a hard database guarantee via a UNIQUE constraint on the trade_id column. For example, if Kafka redelivers trade TRD-A1B2 after a rebalance, `existsByTradeId("TRD-A1B2")` returns true and we skip it, so Rajesh is never settled twice.

A Dead Letter Topic handles poison messages — events that keep failing no matter how many times you retry. In Spring Kafka, `@RetryableTopic(attempts = "3", backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2), dltTopicSuffix = "-dlt")` automatically creates retry topics and a final dead letter topic. A failing message moves from trade-events to trade-events-retry-0, then retry-1 with growing backoff, and finally to trade-events-dlt. A method annotated with `@DltHandler` then logs and parks it for a human. For example, `public void handleDlt(ConsumerRecord<String,?> record)` records the failed offset so operations can investigate.

At the senior level, a few nuances matter. Setting `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` above 1 is safe for ordering only because idempotence is enabled; without idempotence, in-flight retries can reorder messages. Consumer lag — the gap between the latest offset and the committed offset — is the number one health metric you monitor in production. Partition count is effectively permanent because increasing it changes key-to-partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering for existing keys, so you size it generously up front. And Kafka Streams lets you do stateful processing like windowed aggregations directly on topics; for instance a `TradeVolumeStream` could count trades per symbol in five-minute windows without any external database.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me set the scene at National Bank of India before we write a single line of code, because the code only makes sense once you feel the real problem.

Problem 1 — The bank's trading desk and its settlement desk cannot keep waiting for each other. When Rajesh buys 100 shares of RELIANCE, the trading system must confirm his order in milliseconds so the screen does not freeze. But actually settling that trade — moving money, recording it in the ledger, updating positions — takes longer and involves a different team. If the trading system had to wait for settlement to finish before replying to Rajesh, every slow settlement would freeze the trading screen for everyone. This is exactly the problem Kafka solves. The producer writes a trade event and immediately moves on; the consumer settles it whenever it is ready. The two desks are decoupled, connected only by a stream of events.

Problem 2 — Trades for the same account must never be processed out of order. Suppose Rajesh first buys shares and then sells them seconds later. If the sell were settled before the buy, the ledger would show a sale of shares he does not yet own. The bank needs a guarantee that, for one account, events are handled in the exact order they happened. This is exactly how Kafka partitions with a message key work. By keying every event on the account id, all of Rajesh's events land on one partition, and a partition is a strictly ordered log, so his buy is always settled before his sell.

Problem 3 — The settlement must never lose a trade, and must never settle the same trade twice. Losing a trade means a customer's order silently vanishes; settling twice means Rajesh is charged twice for one purchase. Networks fail, servers restart, and Kafka may redeliver a message after a consumer crash. This is exactly why we combine durable producer settings with an idempotent consumer. acks=all and broker idempotence stop data loss on the way in; a UNIQUE constraint on trade_id and an existence check stop double settlement on the way out.

Problem 4 — Some trades are simply broken and will never succeed. Maybe an event references an account that was closed, or carries corrupted data. Retrying such a poison message forever would block the whole partition behind it and page the on-call engineer endlessly. This is exactly what a Dead Letter Topic is for. After three retries with increasing delays, the broken message is moved aside into a dead letter topic where a human can inspect it, while the healthy stream keeps flowing.

Now that the problems are clear, here is what the mini-project will build. There is a producer application with a TradeEvent record modelling the trade, a TradeEventProducer service that publishes keyed by account id with durable settings, a TradePublishController exposing a REST endpoint to publish a trade, and a KafkaProducerConfig that declares the six-partition topic. There is a consumer application with a Settlement JPA entity and its database table carrying a UNIQUE trade_id, a SettlementRepository with an existsByTradeId method, a SettlementService that performs the idempotency check and saves the settlement inside a transaction, a SettlementListener annotated with KafkaListener and RetryableTopic that consumes events and commits offsets manually, and a DltHandler that catches messages which exhausted all retries. Docker Compose spins up Kafka, Zookeeper, and PostgreSQL so the whole thing runs locally. Each part maps directly to one of the four problems above.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a single trade that Rajesh places from his savings account. He buys 100 shares of RELIANCE at 2450.50 rupees each. So the input data is accountId SAV2001, symbol RELIANCE, side BUY, quantity 100, and price 2450.50. The total amount will be 245050.00 rupees. Let us follow this trade from the moment it is published until it is safely settled in the database.

Step 1 — The request arrives at the producer. Rajesh's action becomes an HTTP POST to the trade producer service at /api/v1/trades/publish with the query parameters above. The TradePublishController receives it. At this point the data lives only in memory as method parameters. Nothing is persisted yet.

Step 2 — The controller builds the event. It generates a trade id such as TRD-A1B2 using a random UUID, and it computes the total amount by multiplying the price 2450.50 by the quantity 100, giving 245050.00 as a BigDecimal. It wraps everything into a TradeEvent record with a timestamp. The data is now a single immutable TradeEvent object in the producer's memory.

Step 3 — The producer publishes to Kafka. The TradeEventProducer calls kafkaTemplate.send with the topic trade-events and, critically, the key SAV2001 which is Rajesh's account id. Kafka hashes this key to pick a partition — say partition 2 — so every event for SAV2001 always lands on the same partition and stays in order. Because acks=all is set, the producer waits until all replicas have stored the message, and because idempotence is enabled, even a retried send will not create a duplicate on the broker. The data now physically sits in the Kafka log on partition 2 at a specific offset, say offset 0.

Step 4 — The consumer receives the event. A consumer in the settlement-group that owns partition 2 polls and gets the record. The SettlementListener.onTradeEvent method is invoked with the record and an Acknowledgment handle. The data is now back in memory, this time inside the consumer process, along with its partition number (2) and offset (0).

Step 5 — The service checks for duplicates. The listener calls SettlementService.settle, which first asks settlementRepo.existsByTradeId("TRD-A1B2"). The database answers false because this trade has never been seen. This idempotency check is what makes at-least-once delivery safe — if Kafka ever redelivers this same event after a rebalance, the answer would be true and we would simply skip it.

Step 6 — The settlement is written to the database. The service creates a Settlement entity with a new settlement id such as STL-C3D4, the trade id TRD-A1B2, account SAV2001, symbol RELIANCE, amount 245050.00, status SETTLED, and the Kafka partition and offset recorded for traceability. The repository saves it inside a transaction. The UNIQUE constraint on trade_id acts as a second safety net against duplicates. The data is now permanently stored in the settlements table.

Step 7 — The offset is committed. Only after the save succeeds does the listener call ack.acknowledge(). This commits the Kafka offset for partition 2, telling the broker "I have safely handled up to offset 0." The order matters: we process first, then commit, which is exactly what at-least-once delivery means. If the consumer had crashed between step 6 and this commit, Kafka would redeliver the event, and step 5 would catch the duplicate.

The final output logged by the consumer looks like this:

```
2026-10-24 20:05:01 [settlement-group-1] INFO  SettlementListener - Received: TRD-A1B2 from partition=2 offset=0
2026-10-24 20:05:01 [settlement-group-1] INFO  SettlementService - Settled: TRD-A1B2 → STL-C3D4 (partition=2, offset=0)

# If the same event is redelivered:
2026-10-24 20:05:03 [settlement-group-1] WARN  SettlementService - DUPLICATE: trade TRD-A1B2 already settled — skipping (at-least-once is safe)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer: POST /api/v1/trades/publish
    │
    ├─ TradeEventProducer.publishTradeEvent()
    │   ├─ KEY = accountId ("SAV2001") → all SAV2001 events go to SAME partition
    │   ├─ acks=all → broker waits for ALL replicas to acknowledge
    │   ├─ enable.idempotence=true → broker deduplicates retries
    │   └─ KafkaTemplate.send("trade-events", "SAV2001", event)
    │
    ▼
  Kafka Cluster (topic: trade-events, 6 partitions, replication=3)
    │
    ├─ Partition 0: [events for accounts hashing to 0]
    ├─ Partition 1: [events for accounts hashing to 1]
    ├─ Partition 2: [SAV2001 events — offset 0, 1, 2, ...]  ← ordered per partition!
    ├─ Partition 3: [CUR3001 events]
    ├─ Partition 4: [...]
    └─ Partition 5: [...]
    │
    ▼
  Consumer Group: "settlement-group" (concurrency=3)
    │
    ├─ Consumer-1: reads Partition 0 + Partition 1
    ├─ Consumer-2: reads Partition 2 + Partition 3  ← handles SAV2001
    └─ Consumer-3: reads Partition 4 + Partition 5
    │
    ▼
  SettlementListener.onTradeEvent(record, ack)
    │
    ├─ IDEMPOTENCY: settlementRepo.existsByTradeId("TRD-A1B2")
    │   ├─ EXISTS: skip (duplicate Kafka delivery — safe!) (Recommended) 
    │   └─ NOT EXISTS: proceed
    │
    ├─ settlementRepo.save(settlement)
    │   └─ INSERT INTO settlements (trade_id UNIQUE constraint = 2nd layer idempotency)
    │
    ├─ ack.acknowledge()  ← MANUAL offset commit (at-least-once)
    │   (If crash BEFORE ack: rebalance replays from last committed offset
    │    → duplicate delivery → idempotency check catches it (Recommended) )
    │
    ▼
  On FAILURE (3 retries with backoff):
    trade-events → trade-events-retry-0 (1s) → trade-events-retry-1 (2s) → trade-events-dlt
    │
    └─ DltHandler: log error, alert ops, store for manual investigation

  ═══ CONSUMER GROUP REBALANCING ═══

  3 consumers, 6 partitions → each gets 2 partitions
  If Consumer-2 dies → rebalance: Consumer-1 gets 3, Consumer-3 gets 3
  If Consumer-4 joins → rebalance: each gets 1-2 partitions
  More consumers than partitions → extras are IDLE (max parallelism = partition count)

  ═══ OFFSET MANAGEMENT ═══

  auto.commit=false + manual ack.acknowledge()
    = AT-LEAST-ONCE: process THEN commit
    If crash after process but before commit → message replayed → idempotent consumer handles it

  auto.commit=true (default — DANGEROUS!)
    = AT-MOST-ONCE: commit THEN process
    If crash after commit but before process → message LOST!
```
sections.s5c_hld:
High-Level Design is the bird's eye view of the whole system. Imagine standing on the roof of a tall building in the city and looking down. You see the buildings (the services), the roads between them (the connections), the power plant (the databases), and the postal service (the message queues). You do not see individual rooms or furniture — that level of detail is Low-Level Design. HLD answers one simple question: what systems exist, and how do they talk to each other? In our case, the system is a trade event platform where a producer publishes trade events, Kafka carries them, and a consumer settles them.

In plain banking words, the bank has a trading front-end where a customer places a buy or sell order. That request goes through a security gate (the API gateway), reaches the producer department (the trade producer service), which drops a letter into the bank's internal mail system (Kafka). The settlement department (the consumer service) picks up the letter, records the settlement in the permanent ledger (PostgreSQL), and keeps a fast lookup copy in a notepad (Redis cache). If a letter cannot be processed even after three tries, it goes into the undeliverable drawer (the Dead Letter Topic) so a human can look at it later. Separately, an audit team and a notification team read copies of the mail to keep logs and send SMS messages.

The client layer is where requests begin — a trading web UI, a mobile app, or an exchange gateway. The API gateway is the front door: it checks the JWT token, enforces rate limits so nobody floods the system, and routes the request to the correct service. The application layer holds the trade producer service and the settlement consumer service, each running as several instances for scale. The producer talks to Kafka asynchronously by producing messages — it does not wait for settlement to finish, which is the whole point of event-driven design. The data layer is PostgreSQL as the source of truth for settlements, with read replicas for heavy reporting queries. The caching layer is Redis, holding account balances and trade status with a short time-to-live so reads are fast. The message queue layer is the Kafka cluster with the trade-events topic split into six partitions, plus retry topics and a Dead Letter Topic. External systems include the stock exchange (NSE/BSE) and payment rails. Observability is handled by Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, the ELK stack for logs, and Jaeger for distributed tracing. Security is JWT at the gateway, TLS in transit, and secrets stored in a vault rather than hardcoded.

sections.s5d_lld:
Low-Level Design is the floor plan of one building. If HLD showed the whole city — the services, the databases, the Kafka cluster — LLD zooms right into the settlement consumer service and shows every class (room), every method (door), every field (furniture), and the design patterns and principles that hold it together. LLD answers: what classes do I create, what methods do they have, how do they connect, and which patterns keep the design clean? In a FAANG interview, after you draw the city map, the interviewer says "now zoom into the settlement service and show me the class design" — and this is that answer.

In plain banking words, the HLD said the settlement department exists and talks to the ledger. LLD now walks inside that department. There is a receptionist (the SettlementListener) who takes each letter from the Kafka mailbox. There is a manager (the SettlementService) who decides whether this letter was already handled, and if not, records it. There is a clerk (the SettlementRepository) who writes into the permanent ledger and checks for duplicates. And there is an overflow desk (the DltHandler) that deals with letters nobody could process after three attempts. Each person has a clear, single job, which is the whole idea behind good design.

```

  │     WHY: at-least-once delivery means duplicates WILL happen      │
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Topics categorize events. Partitions provide parallelism — one partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a group. The message key determines the partition (same key always goes to the same partition), which guarantees ordering per key. Producer acks=all with idempotence enabled ensures no data loss and no duplicates at the broker level.

In my banking trade settlement platform, the producer publishes trade events keyed by accountId, ensuring all events for one account are ordered in the same partition. The consumer group has 3 consumers for 6 partitions — each consumer handles 2 partitions. Manual offset commit (ack.acknowledge after processing) provides at-least-once delivery. The consumer is idempotent: a UNIQUE constraint on trade_id and an existsByTradeId check prevent duplicate settlements when Kafka replays messages after a rebalance. RetryableTopic automatically retries failed messages with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s) and moves poison pills to a Dead Letter Topic for manual investigation. Schema evolution would use Avro with Schema Registry to ensure backward-compatible changes between producer and consumer deployments.

---

keyPoints: Dead Letter Topic (DLT): store failed messages for later analysis
Retry topic: automatic retry with backoff before DLT
Poison pill: message that always fails — skip or DLT
